meta.title: Who really said "It is amazing what you can accomplish if you do not care who gets the credit"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Harry S. Truman. The earliest record is an English Jesuit, Father Strickland, quoted in Grant Duff's diary on 21 September 1863 and printed in 1897.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It is amazing what you can accomplish if you do not care who gets the credit'?
meta.ogDescription: Truman never said it on any record. The line traces to Father Strickland in 1863; the earliest Truman credit is a Time column of 7 November 1988.

answer.label: Not Harry S. Truman — a reworking of an 1863 remark
answer.authorDates: fl. 1863 · English Jesuit priest, quoted in Grant Duff’s diary
answer.sourceLine: No record from Truman’s lifetime has him saying this. Quote Investigator ↗ traces the thought to an English Jesuit named Father Strickland, whose remark Sir Mountstuart E. Grant Duff wrote into his diary on 21 September 1863; the earliest credit to Truman it has found is a Time column of 7 November 1988. The familiar “it is amazing what you can accomplish” phrasing is a twentieth-century reshaping, not Strickland’s words and not Truman’s.

source.excerpt: September · 21. Met at the house of the Rev. C. K. Paul, at Stourminster Marshall, Father Strickland, an English Jesuit, who said to me—“I have observed, throughout life, that a man may do an immense deal of good, if he does not care who gets the credit for it.”
trail: 1863, spoken. Father Strickland’s remark, written into Grant Duff’s diary and printed in 1897 at p. 237 ↗.
1905–1922, drifting. Versions credited in turn to Benjamin Jowett, Edward Everett Hale and C. E. Montague, with Quote Investigator ↗ tracking each reassignment.
1982, on a desk. The variant on Reagan’s Oval Office sign, filmed by White House Television on 25 September 1982 ↗.

1988, pinned to Truman. Time’s Hugh Sidey gives the modern wording to Harry S. Truman on 7 November 1988 — the earliest such credit Quote Investigator ↗ has located, and the point from which the quote databases copy.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the scanned first edition, where the day number sits under a “September” month heading. The place name is printed as “Stourminster Marshall.” Note the wording: this is not the popular sentence, which reshapes the thought roughly a century later.

author.name: Father Strickland
author.kicker: The man the line actually belongs to
author.heading: About Father Strickland
author.metaLine: fl. 1863 · English Jesuit priest · recorded by Sir Mountstuart E. Grant Duff
author.bio: Almost nothing is documented about him beyond a single evening. On 21 September 1863, at the house of the Rev. C. K. Paul in Dorset, an English Jesuit whom the diarist names only as Father Strickland told Sir Mountstuart E. Grant Duff that a man may do an immense deal of good if he does not care who gets the credit for it. Grant Duff — a Liberal MP, later Governor of Madras, and a compulsive recorder of other people’s good lines — kept the sentence in his notebook for thirty-four years before publishing it, which is the only reason we have it at all. Quote Investigator identifies him as the key progenitor of the whole family of sayings that eventually reached Truman’s name.

misattribution.heading: Who has been given the credit for “who gets the credit”
misattribution.intro: For a sentence about not needing credit, this one has been handed around a great deal. Here is who has held it, and on what evidence.

items.scope: The whole quote, in this wording
items.why: Nothing from Truman’s lifetime carries it. Quote Investigator ↗ reports it has “not found any substantial support” for the attribution, and dates the earliest Truman credit to Hugh Sidey’s column in Time, 7 November 1988. Wikiquote ↗ lists it under “Misattributed.”

Reagan kept a sign on the Oval Office desk reading “There is no limit to what a man can do or where he can go if he doesn’t mind who gets the credit” — filmed by White House Television on 25 September 1982 ↗. He popularised the wording; the sentiment was already more than a century old.

Edward T. Cook credited Jowett in 1905 with “the way to get things done is not to mind who gets the credit of doing them,” then reassigned it in 1909 to “a wise man” and in 1911 to a “Jesuit Father” — per Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗.

items.who: Edward Everett Hale and C. E. Montague
items.why: Both used versions in the decades after 1893, and Montague explicitly credited his to someone else rather than claiming it, according to Quote Investigator ↗.
Its public Truman Quotes page ↗ presents the line as Truman’s with no source attached — one reason the attribution keeps regenerating.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented form belongs to Father Strickland, an English Jesuit, speaking on 21 September 1863 and printed in Grant Duff’s Notes from a Diary, 1851–1872, vol. 1, p. 237 ↗: “a man may do an immense deal of good, if he does not care who gets the credit for it.”

context.heading: Why this one stuck to Truman
lead: The saying travelled for a century and a quarter before it landed on a president. Grant Duff heard it from a Jesuit in 1863 and printed it in 1897; Edward Everett Hale, Benjamin Jowett and C. E. Montague were each credited with versions of it over the following decades; a coaching magazine and a Kansas state legislator were using the modern “it’s amazing what you can accomplish” shape in the 1970s and early 1980s. Nobody needed Truman for any of that.

What Truman supplied was plausibility. A plain-spoken president who kept THE BUCK STOPS HERE on his desk is exactly the sort of person the line sounds like — and once Time attached his name to it in 1988, quotation databases copied it forward without ever asking what he had supposedly been saying, or to whom, or when. The Truman Library Institute’s own quotations page runs it today with no source attached.
detailsBody: 1863 — Father Strickland to Grant Duff: “a man may do an immense deal of good, if he does not care who gets the credit for it.” Published 1897.
1905–1911 — Edward T. Cook credits a version to Benjamin Jowett, then reassigns it to “a wise man,” then to a “Jesuit Father,” per Quote Investigator’s chronology.
1982 — White House Television films the sign on Ronald Reagan’s Oval Office desk: “There is no limit to what a man can do or where he can go if he doesn’t mind who gets the credit.”
1988 — Hugh Sidey’s Time column gives the modern wording to Harry S. Truman — the earliest such credit Quote Investigator has located.
context.pull: The sentence is real, old, and worth keeping. The name on it is the only fabricated part.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator traces this saying to Father Strickland (21 September 1863, recorded by Grant Duff in Notes from a Diary, 1851-1872, published 1897), states it has "not found any substantial support" for the Truman attribution, and dates the earliest Truman credit to Hugh Sidey in Time, 7 November 1988; it also documents the Jowett 1905/1909/1911 reassignments, a 1975 Scholastic Coach citation, a 1982 Lawrence Journal-World citation, and Reagan's desk plaque.

Wikiquote lists "It is amazing what you can accomplish if you do not care who gets the credit" under its "Misattributed" section for Harry S. Truman, noting a similar saying is recorded as early as 1863 and linking to Quote Investigator.

Page 237 of Grant Duff's Notes from a Diary, 1851-1872, vol. 1, carries the September 21 entry: "Met at the house of the Rev. C. K. Paul, at Stourminster Marshall, Father Strickland, an English Jesuit, who said to me - 'I have observed, throughout life, that a man may do an immense deal of good, if he does not care who gets the credit for it.'"
The Internet Archive hosts a scan of volume 1 of Mountstuart E. Grant Duff's Notes from a Diary, 1851-1872, published London: John Murray, 1897.

The Reagan Library holds a White House Television record dated 25 September 1982 titled "Cuts of Oval Office Desk and sign 'There is no limit to what a man can do or where he can go if he doesn't mind who gets the credit.'"
WIST Quotations classes the Truman attribution of this line as spurious, notes no contemporary evidence, and names a 1988 Time article by Hugh Sidey as the earliest attribution to Truman.
The Truman Library Institute's Truman Quotes page presents "It is amazing what you can accomplish if you do not care who gets the credit." as a Harry S. Truman quotation with no source given.
